## Part 1: Foundations

### Ch. 1 Introduction ★ · [p. 56–91](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=56) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/01_introduction/01_introduction.html)

**Master.** Why data-defined behaviour can degrade while code is unchanged. The D·A·M lens for finding bottlenecks. The iron law (memory + compute + overhead). The Bitter Lesson and when extra compute pays off. Three kinds of efficiency (algorithmic, compute, data selection).
**Read with.** The introduction to @sec-sys-cs249r. Part III, *The learning problem*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why can an ML system fail \"silently\"?"}
Its behaviour is defined by data, not by code. When the input distribution moves away from the training data, predictions degrade even though every service is up and no code changed. Availability metrics stay green while quality drops, so you need quality and drift monitoring, not just uptime.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Use the iron law to explain why a 2× faster GPU may not halve inference time."}
$T = D/BW + O/(R\eta) + L$. A faster compute unit shrinks only the compute term. If the workload is memory-bound or overhead-bound (small batches, many small kernels, network hops), the other two terms dominate and the end-to-end speed-up is small (Amdahl's law).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What are the three dimensions of ML efficiency?"}
Algorithmic efficiency (fewer FLOPs per unit of accuracy, through better architectures and compression), compute efficiency (more useful FLOPs per second and per joule, through hardware and kernels), and data efficiency (more accuracy per sample, through selection, deduplication, and curricula). Each one changes a different factor of the iron law.
:::

### Ch. 2 System Paradigms · [p. 100–156](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=100) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/02_system_paradigms/02_system_paradigms.html)

**Master.** The four deployment regimes (cloud, edge, mobile, TinyML) span about nine orders of magnitude in compute and power. Which physical constraint binds in each. Choosing a regime by privacy, latency, resources, and cost. Hybrid cloud–edge patterns.
**Read with.** Part XVI, *ML system design* (choosing where the model runs).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: When would you run a model on-device rather than in the cloud?"}
When latency must be very low or the device must work offline, when the data is private and must stay on the device, when bandwidth or connectivity is limited, or when per-request cloud cost is too high at scale. The price is tight memory, compute and energy budgets, so small or compressed models and harder updates.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Give an example of a hybrid architecture."}
A wake-word detector runs on a microcontroller (TinyML, always on, microwatts) and wakes a larger on-phone model, which sends hard queries to a cloud LLM. Each tier filters traffic so the expensive tier sees only a small fraction of it.
:::

### Ch. 3 ML Lifecycle · [p. 160–201](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=160) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/03_ml_lifecycle/03_ml_lifecycle.html)

**Master.** The six stages (problem definition → data → model → evaluation → deployment → monitoring) form a loop with feedback. How ML workflows differ from ordinary software. Stating the problem as a measurable improvement over a baseline. How a constraint discovered late cascades into rework.
**Read with.** Part IV, *An end-to-end ML project*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What is the constraint propagation principle?"}
A decision or constraint at one stage (for example, "must run in 20 ms on a phone") propagates to every later stage: the data that can be used, which models are feasible, how validation is done, and how deployment works. A constraint found late forces rework of everything that depended on it, so constraints must be captured at problem definition.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How is ML development different from ordinary software development?"}
ML behaviour comes from data, so it drifts as data changes. Training can be non-deterministic. "Correct" is statistical, not exact. Testing needs held-out data and slice metrics as well as unit tests. Production feedback (monitoring and retraining) is part of the system, not an afterthought.
:::

### Ch. 4 Data Engineering · [p. 204–287](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=204) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/04_data_engineering/04_data_engineering.html)

**Master.** Data as source code and "data cascades". Acquisition strategies. Batch vs streaming ingestion and validation. Labelling. Leakage-safe transformations. Training–serving consistency. Data gravity and storage bandwidth. File formats and loaders that keep the accelerator fed. Drift and data debt.
**Read with.** Part IV, *Feature engineering and data cleaning*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What is training–serving skew, and how do you prevent it?"}
Features are computed differently at training time (batch, offline) and at serving time (online), so the model sees a different input distribution in production. Prevent it with one shared feature definition (a feature store, or the same transformation code), logging served features and training on those logs, and parity tests that compare offline and online feature values for the same entity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why do columnar formats and sharded records matter for training?"}
Training reads large datasets sequentially, many times over. Columnar formats (Parquet) let you read only the needed columns and compress well. Packing many small samples into large shards (TFRecord, WebDataset) avoids per-file overhead and enables sequential, prefetchable reads, so the GPU doesn't stall waiting for I/O.
:::

## Part 2: Build

### Ch. 5 Neural Computation · [p. 296–367](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=296) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/05_nn_computation/05_nn_computation.html)

**Master.** Activations and their hardware cost. Counting parameters, MACs, and activation memory. How batching raises arithmetic intensity. Forward and backward passes as batched matrix operations. Training vs inference workloads. An end-to-end digit-recognition pipeline.
**Read with.** Part II, *Linear algebra* and *Matrix calculus*. Part VII, *Neural networks* and *Backpropagation*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How many parameters and MACs does a dense layer from 1024 to 4096 have, at batch size 32?"}
Parameters: $1024\times4096 + 4096 = 4{,}198{,}400$. MACs: $32\times1024\times4096\approx134$ M (about 268 MFLOPs). The weights are read once per batch, so a larger batch raises FLOPs per byte (arithmetic intensity).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why does training need much more memory than inference?"}
Training stores activations for the backward pass, the gradients, and the optimizer state. Adam keeps two moments per parameter, often in fp32. Inference needs only the weights and transient activations, plus a KV cache for LLMs.
:::

### Ch. 6 Network Architectures · [p. 372–452](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=372) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/06_nn_architectures/06_nn_architectures.html)

**Master.** Inductive bias for each data type. How MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, Transformers, and DLRM-style recommenders lower to matrix multiplication, and which of their operations stay memory-bound. What skip connections and normalization cost. Counting weights, MACs, and memory for each layer type. Transformer prefill vs decode.
**Read with.** Parts VII–IX (architectures). Part XIV, *Recommender systems* (embedding tables).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why are recommendation models (DLRM) often memory-bound?"}
They are dominated by huge embedding tables (often many GB to TB) that are read sparsely: a few rows per feature per example, gathered from random locations. Gathers have almost no arithmetic per byte, so throughput depends on memory capacity and bandwidth. The dense MLP part is small by comparison.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How do transformer prefill and decode differ?"}
Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel, with many tokens per weight read, so it is compute-bound and it fills the KV cache. Decode generates one token per step per sequence and re-reads all the weights and the KV cache, so it is memory-bandwidth-bound. Serving systems schedule and size these two phases differently.
:::

### Ch. 7 ML Frameworks · [p. 456–536](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=456) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/07_frameworks/07_frameworks.html)

**Master.** Eager, graph, and JIT-compiled execution (dispatch overhead, kernel fusion). Reverse-mode autodiff and which forward state it saves. Tensor layout, dtype, and device placement. Module abstractions. Whether a training step is bound by dispatch, memory traffic, or arithmetic. PyTorch vs JAX vs TensorFlow.
**Read with.** Part I, *PyTorch fundamentals*. Part II, *Matrix calculus and autodiff*. Part VII, *Backpropagation*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What does `torch.compile` / XLA buy you over eager mode?"}
It captures a graph of operations, which allows kernel fusion: several elementwise operations become one kernel, so intermediates stay in fast memory and the number of launches drops. It also allows memory planning and fewer Python dispatches. The gains are largest for many small, memory-bound operations. The costs are compile time and recompilation when shapes change.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why is reverse mode used for training rather than forward mode?"}
A loss is a scalar function of many parameters. Reverse mode gets the full gradient in one backward pass, at about the cost of 2–3 forward passes. Forward mode would need one pass per input direction. The price of reverse mode is storing (or recomputing) intermediate activations.
:::

### Ch. 8 Model Training ★ · [p. 540–633](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=540) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/08_training/08_training.html)

**Master.** Training cost: FLOPs, time, energy, activation memory, optimizer state, and dollars. SGD vs Adam vs AdamW, including their memory cost. Prefetching, overlap, and checkpointing. Diagnosing whether a run is compute-, memory-, or data-bound with MFU. Mixed precision, FlashAttention, gradient accumulation, and activation checkpointing. When one node is no longer enough.
**Read with.** Part VII, *Optimizers for deep learning*, *Normalization*, *The training recipe*. Part XII, *Scaling laws and compute*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How much memory does it take to train a 7B model with Adam in mixed precision, excluding activations?"}
A common accounting is 16 bytes per parameter: bf16 weights (2) + bf16 gradients (2) + fp32 master weights (4) + Adam $m$ (4) + Adam $v$ (4). For 7B parameters that is about 112 GB, more than one 80 GB GPU holds. Hence sharded optimizers (ZeRO/FSDP), 8-bit optimizers, or offloading.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What does activation checkpointing trade?"}
It stores activations only at checkpoint boundaries and recomputes the rest during the backward pass. Activation memory drops from $O(L)$ to about $O(\sqrt{L})$ with optimal spacing, at the cost of roughly one extra forward pass (about 20–33% more compute).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What is MFU, and what is a good value?"}
Model FLOPs Utilization is the useful model FLOPs per second (for example $6N\cdot$tokens/s) divided by the hardware peak. Recomputation does not count as useful. Well-tuned large-scale LLM training typically reaches about 35–55%. Low MFU points to data stalls, communication, small kernels, or poor parallelism.
:::

## Part 3: Optimize

### Ch. 9 Data Selection · [p. 644–706](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=644) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/09_data_selection/09_data_selection.html)

**Master.** Data selection as data–algorithm co-design. The compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter check (about 20 tokens per parameter in Chinchilla). When selection overhead pays off. Deduplication, coresets, and quality pruning. Curricula, active learning, and synthetic data. Keeping the pipeline fed.
**Read with.** Part XII, *Pretraining data*. Part IV, *Learning with few labels*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why deduplicate pretraining data?"}
Duplicates waste compute on repeated samples, increase memorisation (and with it privacy and copyright risk), skew the data mixture, and can contaminate evaluation sets. Near-duplicate detection (MinHash/LSH) is a standard step in pretraining pipelines.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: When is a data-selection method worth it?"}
When the compute saved by training on fewer or better samples, plus any accuracy gained, is worth more than the cost of scoring and selecting the data. Scoring every sample with a large model can cost more than it saves. The trade looks better when the selection is reused across many runs.
:::

### Ch. 10 Model Compression ★ · [p. 710–803](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=710) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/10_model_compression/10_model_compression.html)

**Master.** Pruning vs distillation vs quantization: which resource each relaxes. Estimating memory, precision, and sparsity savings. Post-training vs quantization-aware vs weight-only quantization. Structured pruning that maps to real kernels. Ordering a compression pipeline. Measuring real latency rather than FLOPs.
**Read with.** Part VII, *Transfer learning and distillation*. Part XII, *LLM inference II (quantization)*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why does unstructured 50% sparsity often give no speed-up?"}
Dense hardware still multiplies the zeros unless there are sparse kernels or a supported pattern (such as 2:4 structured sparsity on NVIDIA). Irregular sparsity also hurts memory-access efficiency. Structured pruning (whole channels, heads, or layers) shrinks the dense matrices and does speed things up.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Compare PTQ and QAT."}
Post-training quantization calibrates scales on a small dataset after training. It is cheap, works well at INT8, and is harder at INT4 or below. Quantization-aware training simulates quantization during training (fake-quant with a straight-through estimator), so the model adapts. It is more accurate at low bit-widths but costs training compute.
:::

### Ch. 11 Hardware Acceleration ★ · [p. 808–921](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=808) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/11_hw_acceleration/11_hw_acceleration.html)

**Master.** Specialising hardware for tensor workloads, and Amdahl's law. Tensor Cores, systolic arrays, SIMD/SIMT. The memory wall and the cache hierarchy. Arithmetic intensity and the roofline model. Dataflow, tiling, and reuse. Compiler fusion and scheduling. Choosing an accelerator.
**Read with.** Part XII, *Efficient attention (FlashAttention tiling)*. @sec-sys-cs249r (iron law).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Explain the roofline model."}
Attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s, arithmetic intensity × memory bandwidth), where arithmetic intensity is FLOPs per byte moved. Kernels left of the ridge point are memory-bound; to speed them up, raise their intensity through fusion, tiling, or larger batches. Kernels right of it are compute-bound; use lower precision or better use of the tensor cores.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why does FlashAttention speed attention up without reducing FLOPs?"}
Standard attention writes the $T\times T$ score matrix to HBM and reads it back. FlashAttention tiles $Q$, $K$ and $V$ into on-chip SRAM and computes the softmax in a streaming fashion with an online rescaling. The scores never touch HBM. Memory traffic drops from $O(T^2)$ to $O(T)$ per head, and since attention was memory-bound, it runs much faster.
:::

### Ch. 12 Benchmarking · [p. 924–1016](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=924) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/12_benchmarking/12_benchmarking.html)

**Master.** The gap between benchmarks and production. Turning a claim into a test (task, data, metrics, harness, rules). Micro, macro, and end-to-end granularity. MLPerf-style training metrics (time to quality) and inference metrics (throughput, latency percentiles). Energy measurement. Statistical significance across repeated runs. Calibration and slice metrics.
**Read with.** Part IV, *Comparing models and A/B testing*, *Calibration*, *Metrics*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why report p99 latency and not just the mean?"}
Users and downstream services feel the tail. In fan-out systems, a request that waits on many calls is likely to hit some slow one. The mean hides queueing spikes, garbage-collection pauses, and cold starts. SLOs are usually set on p95 or p99.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How do you know a 2% speed-up is real?"}
Repeat the runs, control for warm-up, thermal state and clocks, use paired comparisons on the same inputs, and report a confidence interval. If the interval excludes zero (and the result survives a change of seed or hardware unit), it is real.
:::

## Part 4: Deploy

### Ch. 13 Model Serving ★ · [p. 1026–1115](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=1026) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/13_model_serving/13_model_serving.html)

**Master.** The serving inversion (from throughput to per-request latency). Breaking down where request latency goes. Queueing laws (Little's law) and capacity planning. Batching windows. Choosing a runtime. Cold starts. LLM serving (token latency, KV-cache memory, continuous batching). Cost per inference.
**Read with.** Part XII, *LLM inference I/II*. Part XVI, *ML system design*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: State Little's law and use it."}
$L=\lambda W$: average requests in the system = arrival rate × average time in the system. At 200 req/s and 50 ms average latency, about 10 requests are in flight, so you need at least that much concurrency, plus headroom because utilisation near 100% makes queueing delay explode.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How does continuous batching improve LLM throughput?"}
Static batching waits until every sequence in a batch finishes, so short sequences leave slots idle. Continuous (in-flight) batching admits new requests and retires finished ones at every decode step, so the batch stays full. Combined with paged KV-cache memory, it typically raises throughput severalfold at the same latency.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: How big is the KV cache?"}
Per token: $2\times n_\text{layers}\times n_\text{kv-heads}\times d_\text{head}\times$ bytes. For a 7B-class model (32 layers, 32 KV heads × 128 dims, bf16) that is $2\cdot32\cdot4096\cdot2$ bytes ≈ 0.5 MB per token, so a 4k-token context is about 2 GB per sequence. GQA and MQA (fewer KV heads) and KV quantization cut this directly.
:::

### Ch. 14 ML Operations ★ · [p. 1120–1212](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=1120) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/14_ml_ops/14_ml_ops.html)

**Master.** Silent degradation under shift. ML technical debt. Model registries, parity tests, and CI/CD for models. Canary, blue-green, shadow, and rollback releases. Layered monitoring and incident response. When to retrain. Operational maturity.
**Read with.** Part IV, *Validation*. Part XIV, *Distribution shift*. Part XVI, *ML debugging and production scenarios*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Compare shadow, canary, and blue-green deployment."}
**Shadow**: the new model receives a copy of live traffic, but its outputs are not served. There is no user risk, and it validates latency and behaviour. **Canary**: a small share of real traffic is served by the new model, with automatic rollback on metric regressions. It catches real-impact issues while limiting the blast radius. **Blue-green**: two full environments, with traffic switched over at once. Rollback is fast, but it needs double capacity.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: What triggers retraining?"}
A fixed schedule (simple, cheap to reason about), drift detected in inputs or predictions, or a drop in measured quality once labels arrive. The choice trades staleness cost against retraining cost. It needs automated validation gates so that a bad retrain is never promoted.
:::

### Ch. 15 Responsible Engineering · [p. 1216–1274](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=1216) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/15_responsible_engr/15_responsible_engr.html)

**Master.** Proxy objectives that drift away from the real goal. Finding responsibility failures with D·A·M. Fairness metrics from confusion matrices and the fairness–accuracy frontier. Per-group release gates and monitoring. Cost and carbon. Model cards, datasheets, lineage, and audit trails. Privacy and compliance.
**Read with.** Part IV, *Interpretability*, *Classification metrics*. Vol 2 ch. 16.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Self-check: Why can't you satisfy calibration and equal error rates across groups at once?"}
When base rates differ between groups, a classifier that is calibrated within each group cannot also have equal false-positive and false-negative rates across groups, except in degenerate cases such as a perfect predictor (Kleinberg et al., Chouldechova). You have to choose which fairness criterion matches the harm you care about.
:::

### Ch. 16 Conclusion · [p. 1280–1302](../cs249r/Machine-Learning-Systems-Vol1.pdf#page=1280) · [online](https://mlsysbook.ai/vol1/16_conclusion/16_conclusion.html)

**Master.** How decisions propagate constraints across the whole stack. The lighthouse models. CS249r's thirteen quantitative principles (p. 1287). Use them as a revision sheet before interviews.
